A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GuardSplat and contain readable methods, equations, experiments, figures, tables, and supplementary material. Content can be matched across renumbering and moves between the main paper and appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original watermarking experiments on Blender and LLFF, including accuracy, reconstruction quality, robustness, efficiency, ablations, pruning tests, and larger-message results.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons, VAE-attack results, and supplementary experiments involving lighting, occlusion, SH noise, and specular rendering.

M1.justification: The core CLIP decoder, SH-offset embedding, and objectives remain unchanged. However, v3's implementation description includes VAE attacks in the distortion layer, and Appendix C.3 introduces SH-noise augmentation and training on randomly masked views of up to 20% for particular robustness scenarios.

E1.justification: Blender and LLFF remain the main benchmarks. v3 adds focused experiments using TensoIR's Lego under different lighting and Shiny's ball for specular fidelity, together with VAE attacks, SH perturbations, and occlusion conditions. These extend the input conditions covered within the same watermarking task.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 substantially broaden evaluated comparators with GaussianMarker and GuardSplat using CIN, SSL, and StegaStamp decoders. Table 1 also adds 3DGS trained on images watermarked by CIN, SSL, DwtDctSvd, and StegaStamp. Existing WateRF + 3DGS is retained under the name 3DGS w/ WateRF.

E3.justification: The main test-view counts, training epochs, batch sizes, and learning rates remain unchanged. New protocols include Bmshj2018 VAE attacks and transferring learned SH offsets between lighting-specific representations in Appendix C.3. The efficiency curve changes from total training time in v1 Figure 3 to watermarking time in v3 Figure 7; total time is presented separately.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands robustness analysis beyond the original image distortions and Gaussian pruning: Table 2 adds VAE removal attacks, Appendix C.3 examines SH noise, lighting, occlusion, and viewing angles, and Appendix C.4 examines specular fidelity with zoomed views. Additional decoder substitutions strengthen the component comparison. Existing embedding, loss, hyperparameter, and pruning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over evaluation views without repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The newly disclosed message sampling procedure does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Many baseline and robustness results are added, including 82.35% GuardSplat accuracy under the VAE attack. Original GuardSplat Table 1 values and supplementary pruning and 64/72-bit results remain unchanged. Existing comparator values are revised: 32-bit 3DGS + HiDDeN SSIM changes from 0.9882 to 0.9682, and WateRF + 3DGS crop accuracy from 95.07% to 89.07%. Reported watermarking time changes from 20 to 10 minutes without an explanation.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation in Equations 1–10 is retained. Neither version introduces a theoretical analysis or proofs that are subsequently added, removed, or substantively revised.

C1.justification: The central contributions and claims about capacity, fidelity, security, and robustness remain. The introduction strengthens the quantified efficiency claim from five minutes for decoder training plus twenty minutes for watermarking to five plus ten minutes.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges a maximum message length of 75 bits imposed by CLIP's token limit. Appendix C.3 newly attributes noise and lighting robustness to SH-noise augmentation and occlusion robustness to masked-view training; Appendix C.4 discusses the risk of altering specular appearance.

D1.justification: v3 adds a direct code-repository link where v1 promises future code availability. It also discloses sampling min(2^NL, 2048) messages for decoder training/testing, gives additional distortion parameters such as blur kernel size, and describes the supplementary relighting and masking procedures. The existing decoder architecture is relocated rather than newly disclosed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion adds NeRFProtector and references covering additional image-watermarking methods, mesh steganography, and generative watermark removal. Its critique of decoder fidelity–capacity tradeoffs broadens from HiDDeN to 2D watermarking methods generally. The overall research positioning remains stable; GaussianMarker was already cited in v1.

P1.justification: v3 makes focused wording and terminology edits, reverses Efficient and Robust in the title, updates affiliations and acknowledgements, and reorganizes supplementary material. Existing implementation explanations move into the main experimental section, while most of the introduction, method, and analysis narrative remains closely matched.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 are substantially expanded and Table 1 gains method-group headings. The appendix performance plot and decoder diagram become main Figures 3 and 5, the timing plot is revised, and v1 Figure 4 is removed. New supplementary Figures S3–S4 show rendering-condition and specular comparisons; the original appendix ablation visuals are retained as S1–S2. These changes substantially reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: Adding GaussianMarker, broader decoder comparisons, and targeted robustness tests makes the empirical case more credible. Code and training disclosures and the explicit capacity limit also improve the paper. The gain is qualified by unexplained timing revisions and an unrevised blanket 72-bit superiority statement in Appendix C.2 that is inconsistent with the newly added GaussianMarker results in Table 1.
